profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a crypto market analytics startup two days after an internal pilot of the AITA Order Book Signal (AITA-OBS) stack produced inconsistent results: the research notebook still reproduces the study finding that Empirical Covariance (EC) is the strongest outlier detector on Bitcoin limit order book replays, but the newly productionized replay job shows weaker performance and unusually low alert volume on the same exchange feed. The meeting sits at the handoff point between research and a business-facing surveillance product ahead of a client demo. The agenda is to diagnose why the replay environment diverges from the study setup, decide the most plausible root cause, and agree on a practical fix and rerun plan. The expected outcome is a shared plan to use the standard benchmark baseline, rerun a comparable day slice, revert to the standard preprocessing pipeline, and prepare a brief explanation for leadership on whether the discrepancy comes from data handling, model behavior, or environment configuration.

members.name: Nina Park
members.expertise: Market microstructure research, anomaly detection benchmarking, backtesting design
members.background: Nina built the original comparative study in Python notebooks and designed the AITA-OBS evaluation framework around replayed Bitcoin limit order book events, model ranking, and strategy-level performance summaries.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve confidence in the original benchmark and suspects the divergence comes from implementation drift during operationalization rather than from the study design itself; she also wants to avoid reopening the methodology before the client demo.
hidden_assumptions: The 'standard benchmark baseline' is the exact research reference setup: one exchange venue, research-cleaned event stream, archived train-calibration split, and notebook-era feature matrix.
A 'full day' of Bitcoin order book data means the UTC day boundary used in her backtest archives and experiment logs.

Reverting to the 'standard preprocessing pipeline' means restoring the research feature-engineering and filtering sequence, including removal of crossed books, zero-volume updates, and notebook scaling steps.
If a rerun 'matches EC,' that means EC preserves its relative ranking advantage and broadly similar return profile versus the comparison models, even if alert counts shift somewhat.

members.name: Omar Delgado
members.expertise: Production data pipelines, surveillance productization, model monitoring and client-facing analytics
members.background: Omar oversees the pipeline that turns exchange feeds into client-ready anomaly alerts and dashboard metrics, and recently had his team wrap the AITA-OBS logic into a scheduled replay job for demos and internal QA.
members.private_state: He wants a practical fix that makes the replay job stable and explainable to customers, and he is quietly concerned that the research setup may rely on assumptions that do not hold in the production feed.
hidden_assumptions: The 'standard benchmark baseline' is the production replay job over the canonical warehouse tables, because that is the only baseline he considers operationally meaningful for a client-facing product.
A 'full day' means the commercial reporting day shown in dashboards, which rolls on Eastern Time to match customer reports.

Reverting to the 'standard preprocessing pipeline' means restoring the shared production transformation layer, including timestamp normalization, top-of-book reconstruction rules, venue harmonization, and default gap-filling for sparse depth updates.

If a rerun 'matches EC,' it should restore roughly expected alert volume and visible anomaly clustering in the replay dashboard, because stable counts are what make the output credible to leadership and clients.

misalignment_points.topic: What the standard benchmark baseline refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly agree to 'use the standard benchmark baseline' before comparing outputs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means the original research benchmark exactly as used in the comparative study notebook, including research-cleaned inputs and archived splits.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar means the production replay job as the reference baseline, using warehouse-standardized inputs and operational transforms.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both work in contexts where one baseline is already treated as the obvious default, so 'standard benchmark baseline' sounds like responsible shorthand rather than a phrase needing unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: Which May 12 trading day is being replayed
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to rerun 'the May 12 full day' to compare EC outputs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means 00:00 to 23:59 UTC on May 12, matching the boundaries used in her archived backtest batches.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar means the dashboard day labeled May 12, which spans 00:00 to 23:59 Eastern Time and therefore maps to a different UTC window.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same date label and the phrase 'full day,' and in fast-moving troubleshooting discussions date boundaries in a 24/7 market are often assumed rather than restated unless timezone issues are already suspected.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the standard preprocessing pipeline
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'revert to the standard preprocessing pipeline' before rerunning EC.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means restoring the research preprocessing path only: feature assembly, notebook scaling, and research-time filtering of malformed book states before model scoring.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar means restoring the broader production preprocessing layer: warehouse transforms, timestamp normalization, book reconstruction defaults, gap-filling, and the feed shaping used before alerts are materialized.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Preprocessing is a broad but familiar label that comfortably bundles many steps, and each person assumes the relevant boundary is obvious from their own workflow, so the mismatch hides inside a shared term.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the rerun to match EC
misalignment_points.surface_form: They converge on checking whether the rerun 'matches EC' before closing the issue.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means EC should retain its top-model status and roughly the same backtest return shape relative to the other thirteen models.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar means EC should restore expected alert counts and recognizable anomaly clusters in the replay dashboard so the output looks operationally stable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both criteria are plausible validations of the same model and 'match EC' functions as efficient team shorthand, so each hears the phrase as confirming their own acceptance test without noticing the other is using a different one.
